\paragraph{Drafter's summary.} logit P(churn) = -1.05 + a sparse linear backbone over 40 inputs (day minutes +2.04 per SD, voicemail plan -0.90, international plan +0.76, international charge +0.71, voicemail messages +0.62, ...) + a service-call x low-day-usage gate + a 4+-calls hinge + an evening-minutes hinge + exactly linear voicemail and state-offset units, all additive in the logit. The gate is a low-day-minutes hinge whose kink moves up with each customer-service call (median 147 day minutes at 0 calls, 220 at 4, 276 at 6), so with the direct day-minutes edge the logit is V-shaped in day minutes and frequent callers with low usage churn. Service calls act only through hinges. Train AUC 0.901, accuracy 0.901.

\paragraph{What resisted explanation.} Nothing structural. Hidden nodes 2627 and 9555 (the always-on service-call encoding) were split so the near-dead state:2/state:44 unit 252 could be its own leaf; 161 and 3861 are identically 0 on train (dead). The gate under-predicts churn for frequent callers with low day usage (CSC$>$=4 and day minutes $<$160: 113 rows, model 0.66 vs empirical 0.88) and over-predicts it for low-usage customers with few calls (CSC$<$4, day minutes $<$120: 476 rows, 0.08 vs 0.05). closed\_\allowbreak{}form\_\allowbreak{}max\_\allowbreak{}abs\_\allowbreak{}err 0.031 is 3-significant-figure rounding on state one-hots (standardised values up to 8); the numeric function is exact.

\subsection{Plain-language summary}\label{app:churn100-s2-c1:plain}
\noindent{\small\textit{AI-assisted draft for review (unverified). Each sentence cites the claims (C01, C02, \ldots) that back it; every cited claim was computed on the model and the training split and passed its automatic checks. Magnitudes are changes in predicted risk for a typical patient; confidence words follow the test-split check and n. The text describes what the model does, not the world.}}\par\smallskip
\paragraph{Summary (drafted).} For a typical customer (in West Virginia, area code 415, no international or voice-mail plan, 1 call to customer service and median usage) the model predicts a chance of leaving of about 1\%; it adds up seven parts: fixed-weight inputs, service calls, a voice-mail discount, heavy evening use, state units, a daytime-calls unit and a small state unit.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C056]}} This part adds up most inputs with fixed weights, and daytime minutes count most: they raise a typical customer's chance of leaving steadily, from under 1\% at 112 to about 13\% at 249 minutes.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C057]}} An international plan takes the chance from about 1\% to about 13\%, a voice-mail plan lowers it to under 1\%, and more voice-mail messages raise it steadily, from about 1\% at 0 to about 5\% at 32 messages.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C058, C067, C059]}} A higher international charge, more evening minutes, a higher evening charge and more night-time minutes also raise it steadily, each by one to two points.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C062, C063, C064, C070]}} Through it, the state moves the chance from about 1\% in West Virginia to about 4\% in California and in Washington, and to under 1\% in Hawaii, Vermont and Colorado (41 to 80 training customers per state).\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C060, C061, C066, C068, C071]}} This part adds up two parts: customer-service calls combined with low daytime use, and a rise from 4 calls upwards.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C111]}} Through it, daytime minutes lower the chance only while they stay below about 170 minutes (between 147 and 216 minutes for different customers), in an uneven way: for a typical customer, from about 38\% at 91 minutes to about 1\% at 352 minutes.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C107]}} With an evening charge above 17.12 US dollars, the chance is lowest at about 154 minutes of daytime use and higher either side: from about 1\% at 112 minutes to about 17\% at 249 minutes, against about 2\% to about 10\% at or below that charge.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C103]}} Customer-service calls add to it from 4 calls upwards, in an uneven way: for a typical such customer, from about 3\% at 0 calls to about 11\% at 4 calls.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C108]}} This part reads the voice-mail plan and a few states: through it, a voice-mail plan lowers a typical customer's chance by less than a point, and customers in states other than Alabama, North Carolina and West Virginia get about 2\% instead of about 1\%.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C125, C126]}} Through this part, evening minutes add nothing until about 239 minutes, then lower the chance steadily; it acts on 885 of 4000 training customers, 165 of whom left, and for the typical customer it acts on, the chance is about 5\% without it and about 4\% with it.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C135, C136]}} This part reads only the state and moves the chance by less than half a point: up in Arizona and Ohio, down in Nevada.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C138, C139, C140]}} This part reads the state and daytime calls: being in Tennessee raises a typical customer's chance from about 1\% to about 2\%, and daytime calls barely change it.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C144, C145]}} This small part moves the chance by less than a tenth of a point, up in Arkansas and Utah.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C150, C153]}}
\paragraph{The whole model.} The model adds up seven parts into one score: fixed-weight inputs, service calls, a voice-mail discount, heavy evening use, state units, a daytime-calls unit and a small state unit.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C056]}} \textit{Evidence.} It is made up of these seven parts (each explained below); the score is their sum, which was checked on all 4000 training customers.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C056]}} Changing one input at a time across the whole model, an international plan takes a typical customer's chance of leaving from about 1\% to about 13\%, and a voice-mail plan lowers it to under 1\%.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C001, C012]}} More customer-service calls raise it in an uneven way, from about 1\% at 0 calls to about 3\% at 3 calls.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C008]}} The model ignores the daytime charge, evening calls, international calls and the night-time charge.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C052, C053, C054, C055]}}
\paragraph{Fixed-weight inputs.} This part adds up most inputs with fixed weights: daytime minutes, an international plan and voice-mail messages raise the chance of leaving, steadily for the minutes and messages, and a voice-mail plan lowers it.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C057, C058, C059, C067]}} \textit{Evidence.} Through it, daytime minutes take a typical customer steadily from under 1\% at 112 to about 13\% at 249 minutes, and an international plan from about 1\% to about 13\%; a voice-mail plan lowers the chance to under 1\%.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C057, C058, C067]}} The state moves it from about 1\% in West Virginia to about 4\% in California and Washington, and to under 1\% in Hawaii and Vermont.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C060, C061, C066, C068]}} Its formula reproduces the part exactly on all 4000 training customers.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C096]}}
\paragraph{Service calls.} This part raises the chance of leaving with calls to customer service, from 4 calls upwards and in an uneven way, and more so for customers with low daytime use; it adds up two parts.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C111, C108, C107]}} \textit{Evidence.} It is made of two parts that are added: calls with low usage, and many service calls.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C111]}} Through it, daytime minutes lower a typical customer's chance only while they stay below about 170 minutes (between 147 and 216 minutes for different customers), in an uneven way, from about 38\% at 91 minutes to about 1\% at 352 minutes.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C107]}} Customer-service calls add to it from 4 calls upwards, in an uneven way: for a typical such customer, from about 3\% at 0 calls to about 11\% at 4 calls.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C108]}} With an evening charge above 17.12 US dollars, the chance is lowest at about 154 minutes of daytime use and higher either side: from about 1\% at 112 minutes to about 17\% at 249 minutes, against about 2\% to about 10\% at or below that charge.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C103]}}
\paragraph{Calls with low usage.} This part raises the chance of leaving for customers with low usage, more so when they call customer service: daytime minutes lower it only while they stay below about 170 minutes (between 147 and 216 minutes for different customers), and calls raise it, both in an uneven way.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C119, C113]}} \textit{Evidence.} It acts on 3121 of 4000 training customers, 402 of whom left; for the typical customer it acts on, it changes the chance by less than a point.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C123]}} Through it, a typical customer's chance falls in an uneven way from about 38\% at 91 minutes of daytime use to about 1\% at 352 minutes, with no further fall past about 170 minutes (between 147 and 216 minutes for different customers).\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C119]}} A higher international charge lowers it only while it stays below about 2.95 US dollars (between 2.95 and 4.34 US dollars for different customers), in an uneven way, from about 3\% to about 1\%.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C121]}} Customer-service calls raise it in an uneven way, from about 1\% at 0 calls to about 3\% at 3 calls.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C113]}} Its formula reproduces the part exactly on all 4000 training customers.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C124]}}
\paragraph{Many service calls.} This part raises the chance of leaving with calls to customer service, adding nothing until about 3 calls, then steadily, except in West Virginia.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C131, C130]}} \textit{Evidence.} It acts on 306 of 4000 training customers, 154 of whom left; for the typical customer it acts on, the chance is about 16\% without it and about 26\% with it.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C132]}} It is switched off in West Virginia: for the typical customer it acts on, being in any other state takes the chance from about 16\% to about 26\%.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C130]}} Its formula reproduces the part exactly on all 4000 training customers.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C133]}}
\paragraph{Voice-mail discount.} This part gives customers with a voice-mail plan a small discount on the chance of leaving.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C125]}} \textit{Evidence.} Through it, a voice-mail plan lowers a typical customer's chance by less than a point, and customers in states other than Alabama, North Carolina and West Virginia get about 2\% instead of about 1\%.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C125, C126]}} Its formula reproduces the part exactly on all 4000 training customers.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C129]}}
\paragraph{Heavy evening use.} This part lowers the chance of leaving a little for customers with heavy evening use: evening minutes add nothing until about 239 minutes, then lower it steadily.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C134]}} \textit{Evidence.} It acts on 885 of 4000 training customers, 165 of whom left; for the typical customer it acts on, the chance is about 5\% without it and about 4\% with it.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C136]}} Through it, evening minutes change nothing until about 239 minutes, then lower a typical customer's chance steadily, from about 1\% at 138 minutes to under 1\% at 266 minutes.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C134]}} Its formula reproduces the part exactly on all 4000 training customers.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C137]}}
\paragraph{State units.} This part adds small state offsets: up in Arizona and Ohio, down in Nevada.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C138, C139, C140]}} \textit{Evidence.} Through it, a typical customer's chance moves by less than half a point: up in Arizona and Ohio, down in Nevada, with Missouri and Massachusetts almost unchanged.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C138, C139, C140, C141, C142]}} Its formula reproduces the part exactly on all 4000 training customers.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C143]}}
\paragraph{Daytime calls and Tennessee.} This part gives customers in Tennessee a small rise in the chance of leaving; daytime calls barely change it.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C144, C145]}} \textit{Evidence.} Through it, being in Tennessee takes a typical customer's chance from about 1\% to about 2\%, and going from 75 to 125 daytime calls barely changes it.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C144, C145]}} Its formula reproduces the part exactly on all 4000 training customers.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C149]}}
\paragraph{Small state unit.} This small part barely changes the chance of leaving: it adds less than a tenth of a point in Arkansas and Utah.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C150, C153]}} \textit{Evidence.} Through it, the chance moves by less than a tenth of a point in Arkansas and Utah, a higher international charge lowers it steadily by even less, and customer-service calls barely move it.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C150, C153, C151, C152]}} Its formula reproduces the part exactly on all 4000 training customers.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C161]}}
\paragraph{Worth checking against what is known.} Worth checking: the state moves the chance by several points (for example California and Washington about 6\% and 5\%, Hawaii under 1\%), based on 41 to 122 training customers per state.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C003, C004, C016]}} Worth checking: the model treats a voice-mail plan as lowering the chance of leaving but more voice-mail messages as raising it.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C012, C005]}} Worth checking: the many-service-calls part is switched off for customers in West Virginia, the state of the typical customer.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C130]}} Worth checking: daytime minutes, the evening charge and the international charge raise the chance through the fixed-weight inputs but lower it through calls with low usage.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C057, C112, C064, C115, C062, C114]}}

\subsection{Coverage}\label{app:churn100-s2-c1:coverage}
Coverage is computed by the current code (the function behind the \texttt{get\_coverage} tool) under these conventions. \emph{Candidate nodes} are all nodes of the explained model state except the output nodes. A candidate node is \emph{covered} when some annotation of the hierarchy (a leaf, or a composition together with its descendants) contains it and all its enabled outgoing edges. \emph{Exact Null} parts, which have no effect on any output for any input, count as covered: nodes with no path to an output over enabled, non-zero-weight edges (disconnected inputs and dead ends), and edges that have zero weight or touch such a node. Compositional coverage is the fraction of required compositions present: every annotation except a single global root containing every output must have a parent; a parentless, childless annotation made only of Null nodes is exempt.

\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Null, disconnected input (24):} \texttt{-10} (state:17), \texttt{-11} (state:18), \texttt{-15} (state:21), \texttt{-16} (state:22), \texttt{-17} (state:23), \texttt{-19} (state:25), \texttt{-26} (state:31), \texttt{-29} (state:34), \texttt{-3} (state:10), \texttt{-34} (state:39), \texttt{-36} (state:40), \texttt{-39} (state:43), \texttt{-49} (state:7), \texttt{-5} (state:12), \texttt{-50} (state:8), \texttt{-51} (state:9), \texttt{-6} (state:13), \texttt{-61} (totalDayCharge), \texttt{-63} (totalEveCalls), \texttt{-67} (totalNightCharge), \texttt{-69} (totalIntlCalls), \texttt{-7} (state:14), \texttt{-8} (state:15), \texttt{-9} (state:16).
\item \textbf{Uncovered nodes:} none.
\item \textbf{Uncovered edges:} none.
\item \textbf{Missing compositions:} none.
\end{itemize}
